items.title: Extend GitLab Duo Agent Platform into your business systems
items.summary: Developers mostly use GitLab Duo Agent Platform where they already work: the IDE, merge requests, and issues. But DevSecOps teams also support the business systems the rest of the company runs on, and those systems break too.In Salesforce, for example, when a validation fails, a callout times out, or a null slips through a trigger, the error gets logged, but the log doesn’t explain the cause. An engineer still has to read the stack trace, find the class in the repository, check what changed recently, and decide whether this is a one-off or a regression. Meanwhile, the business user who hit the error has to wait.When your Salesforce metadata lives in GitLab and ships through GitLab CI/CD, the code that explains the error is already there. In this tutorial, Salesforce calls a custom GitLab Duo Agent Platform flow through the Flows API the moment an error happens. The flow investigates the code, and your team gets a GitLab issue that already contains the root-cause analysis.Along the way, three parts of the GitLab platform work together: GitLab Duo Agent Platform investigates the error, a GitLab issue tracks the work, and GitLab CI/CD runs the flow and ships the fix.Salesforce is the example we’ll walk through in this tutorial, but the same approach works for any system that can make an HTTP request.What you'll buildSalesforce makes one call to GitLab. A custom flow in GitLab Duo Agent Platform does the rest.Errors reach GitLab Duo Agent Platform automatically from your Apex error handling, or on demand from a button. Either way, the same Apex job calls the Flows API, and the flow opens an issue with its analysis.PrerequisitesGitLab Premium or Ultimate, on GitLab.com or GitLab 19.5 and later. The Flows API used in this tutorial is generally available from 19.5.GitLab Duo Agent Platform turned on, with custom flows allowed for your top-level group.Your Salesforce metadata (Apex classes, triggers, Flows) stored in a GitLab project. This is the project the flow will read.A Maintainer or Owner role in that project.In Salesforce, permission to create a Named Credential, a custom metadata type, and Apex classes.Your Salesforce deployments must be running through a GitLab CI/CD pipeline, so the fix can ship from the same issue.Step 1: Write the triage flowStart in GitLab, because Salesforce will need the flow's ID later.A custom flow is one YAML file in the flow registry v1 syntax. This one has a single agent. When Salesforce starts the flow, it sends the error details as the flow's goal. The agent reads them as context:goal, investigates the repository, and opens one issue.version: "v1"environment: ambientcomponents:  - name: "sf_error_triage"    type: AgentComponent    prompt_id: "sf_error_triage_prompt"    inputs:      - from: "context:project_id"        as: "project_id"      - from: "context:goal"        as: "error_report"    toolset:      - "find_files"      # locate the class or Flow in the repository      - "grep"      - "read_file"      - "list_commits"    # find recent changes to that file      - "create_issue"    # the only write: open the triage issueprompts:  - prompt_id: "sf_error_triage_prompt"    prompt_template:      system: |        You triage Salesforce runtime errors for a team that keeps its        Salesforce metadata (Apex classes, triggers, Flows) in this project.        You receive an error report with a class name, exception type,        message and stack trace.        1. Find the source file for the class or Flow named in the report.        2. Read the code around the lines in the stack trace.        3. List recent commits that touched that file and identify any change           that plausibly introduced the error.        4. Create one issue:           - Title: "[Salesforce error] <exception type> in <class>"           - Label: salesforce-error           - Description: the original error, then sections for             Likely cause, Affected component, Suspect change,             Suggested next step, and Confidence (high, medium or low,             with one line of reasoning).        Rules:        - Cite file paths, line numbers and commit SHAs for every claim.        - If you cannot find the code or a suspect commit, say so. Do not guess.        - Do not change code. A person decides what happens next.      user: |        Project ID: {{project_id}}        Error report:        {{error_report}}      placeholder: historyrouters:  - from: "sf_error_triage"    to: "end"flow:  entry_point: "sf_error_triage"The toolset is deliberately narrow: four tools read and one creates an issue. The flow can't push code or change existing issues, which makes it easy to review and easy to trust.Two lines in the prompt do the most work. Requiring a citation for every claim lets an engineer check the reasoning in a minute. Allowing "not found" stops the agent from inventing a cause.To create the flow, go to your project, select AI > Flows > New flow, choose Flow, paste the YAML, and select Create flow. You can als
